key_insight: Better retrieval metrics (e.g., higher ColBERT recall) do not automatically produce better answers in RAG systems for AI policy QA — retrieval gains can be misaligned with factuality, helpfulness, and hallucination rates of final LLM responses.
problem_solved: Investigates whether improvements in retrieval components translate to improved downstream answer quality in complex, dense AI policy documents, revealing gaps between retrieval performance and real-world QA reliability.
method: Assembled a RAG pipeline over the AGORA corpus (947 curated AI policy docs) using a ColBERT-based retriever and candidate reranking.
Systematically compared retriever variants, chunking strategies, and prompting configurations, measuring both retrieval metrics and end-task QA outcomes.
Evaluated with automatic metrics and expert human annotations focused on factuality, hallucination, and practical utility for policy analysis.
impact: Alerts ML/AI practitioners that optimizing retrieval alone is insufficient for trustworthy RAG in high-stakes domains; end-to-end evaluation and alignment (retrieval-aware prompting, grounding, calibration, or joint training) are required to improve answer reliability.
visual_elements: RAG pipeline diagram (retriever → reranker → LLM → answer) annotated to show where retrieval improvements may not affect answer quality.
Scatter plot: retrieval score (x-axis) vs answer correctness/factuality (y-axis) showing weak/no correlation.
Bar chart comparing retrieval metrics (recall/MRR) against downstream QA metrics (accuracy/hallucination rate) for different retriever setups.
Annotated example: policy excerpt, retrieved passages, and LLM answer with highlighted errors/unsupported claims.
paper_title: Retrieval Improvements Do Not Guarantee Better Answers: A Study of RAG for AI Policy QA
paper_authors: Saahil Mathur, Ryan David Rittner, Vedant Ajit Thakur, Daniel Stuart Schiff, Tunazzina Islam
